pages.text: For three months, Yousef had spent every spare moment in his grandfather's garage, surrounded by wires, motors and half-eaten bags of sunflower seeds. His goal was simple to explain but almost impossible to achieve: he wanted to build a robot that could climb a date palm and pollinate it on its own. Every spring, the farm in Al-Ahsa hired skilled climbers to do this delicate work by hand, but there were fewer of them each year. If Yousef succeeded, his robot could enter the national youth innovation competition in Riyadh. He had already given it a name, Saqr, after the falcon that never misses its target.

His grandfather, Abu Khalid, was less impressed. He had climbed palms for over fifty years with nothing but a thick rope belt called a karr and his own bare feet. "A machine cannot feel the tree," he said one evening, sipping his cardamom coffee. "The bark changes from palm to palm, and a good climber reads it like a book." Yousef bit his tongue, because arguing with his grandfather was like arguing with the wind. Instead, he promised himself that Saqr would prove him wrong.

The first real test took place on a still, golden morning in March. Saqr wrapped its metal arms around the trunk, and for a few glorious seconds it moved upwards exactly as Yousef had planned. Then, about two metres up, its grip slipped on a patch of rough, uneven bark. The robot slid down the trunk with a horrible scraping sound and landed in the sand with one arm bent at an impossible angle. Yousef stared at it, feeling as if all his hard work had been thrown away in an instant.

That night, he couldn't sleep, so he scrolled through videos of climbing robots from around the world. Most of them had been designed for smooth poles or modern buildings, not for the twisted, scaly trunk of a date palm. The competition deadline was only three weeks away, and he was running out of ideas as quickly as he was running out of time. "Back to the drawing board," he muttered, although he wasn't sure he even had a drawing board left. Eventually, he fell asleep with his phone still glowing on his chest.

When he walked into the garage the next morning, he froze in surprise. His grandfather was sitting on an upturned crate, holding Saqr's damaged arm and studying it under a torch. Beside him lay his old karr, its rope worn smooth by decades of use. "Your machine holds the tree like a frightened child," Abu Khalid said without looking up. "It squeezes too hard in the wrong places, and not at all where it matters."

Over the next hour, the old man explained something Yousef had never noticed. A skilled climber doesn't grip the trunk with constant force; he leans back into the belt, letting it tighten and loosen with each movement. The tension shifts like a heartbeat, adjusting to every bump in the bark. Yousef's eyes widened as the idea took shape in his mind. If Saqr used a flexible strap with pressure sensors, it could copy exactly what his grandfather's body had been doing for half a century.

The following weeks were a blur of late nights, burnt fingertips and countless cups of tea. Abu Khalid, who claimed he understood nothing about computers, turned up in the garage every evening with suggestions about angles and balance. He even climbed a young palm one afternoon so that Yousef could film the way his weight moved. Little by little, the new strap system began to work, and Saqr climbed higher with each test. By the end, the robot was reaching the crown of the tree, where the date flowers grew, without a single slip.

In Riyadh, the judges watched in silence as Saqr climbed a real palm trunk that had been set up in the exhibition hall. When it reached the top and gently released the pollen, the audience broke into applause. One judge asked Yousef how he had solved a problem that engineers in many countries had struggled with. Yousef glanced at the front row, where his grandfather sat in his best thobe, trying not to look proud. "I didn't solve it alone," he said. "I learned it from the best climber in Al-Ahsa."

Saqr won second place, along with a grant to develop the design further. Back at the farm, Yousef added a small engraved plate to the robot's strap that read "The Abu Khalid Grip." His grandfather pretended to find it silly, but Yousef noticed him running his fingers over the letters when he thought no one was watching. That spring, the old man and the robot worked side by side among the palms, one with rope and the other with sensors. "Perhaps a machine can feel the tree after all," Abu Khalid admitted, "as long as someone teaches it how."

stories.title: The Boy Who Helped Measure the World

pages.text: Yusuf had never imagined that a man could measure the whole world without leaving his own neighbourhood. Yet that was exactly what his teacher, the great scholar Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, intended to do. It was the early eleventh century, and they were living in the fort of Nandana, high above a wide, dusty plain in what is now Pakistan. Most of the soldiers at the fort thought the old man was slightly eccentric, because he spent his nights staring at the stars instead of sleeping. Yusuf, who was fifteen and had been his apprentice for two years, was beginning to suspect they were wrong.

One morning al-Biruni called him into his small room, which was crowded with scrolls, maps and strange brass instruments. "Bring the astrolabe," he said, "and please try not to drop it this time." Yusuf blushed, remembering the incident the week before, and carefully lifted the heavy brass disc. "Today," his teacher announced, "we are going to find out how big the Earth is." Yusuf frowned and said, "But surely the scholars in Baghdad did that long ago, didn't they?" "They did," al-Biruni replied, "but the caliph's men needed weeks in the desert with ropes and camels, whereas I intend to do it in a single afternoon, from the top of a mountain."

Before they could climb anything, however, they had to work out exactly how high the mountain was. All morning, Yusuf counted his steps across the burning plain while his teacher measured the angle to the summit from two different points. By midday, sweat was running into Yusuf's eyes and his patience was wearing thin. "Teacher, couldn't we just guess the height?" he asked, wiping his face with his sleeve. Al-Biruni gave him a look that was half amused and half disappointed. "A guess is only a wish dressed up as knowledge," he said, "so let us measure it again, just to be certain."

In the afternoon they began the climb, following a narrow goat path that twisted up the rocky slope. Halfway up, a loose stone rolled beneath Yusuf's foot and he lost his balance. For one terrible moment the astrolabe slipped from his grip, and his heart was in his mouth as it slid towards the edge. Throwing himself forward, he caught it just before it disappeared into the valley below. When he finally stood up, trembling, al-Biruni simply nodded and said, "Good. Now you understand why I asked you not to drop it."

By the time they reached the summit, a thick yellow haze had drifted across the plain. The horizon, which should have been a sharp line, had vanished into a blur of dust and cloud. Yusuf's heart sank, because he realised that if the haze did not clear, the whole exhausting day would have been wasted. His teacher, however, did not seem worried at all; he calmly laid out his prayer mat, prayed Asr, and then sat down on a rock to wait. "The sky does not hurry for anyone," he murmured, "not even for scientists."

Then, just as the sun began to lower, a cool wind swept up from the valley and blew the haze away. Suddenly the horizon appeared again, a perfect line where the earth met the sky, stretching for miles in every direction. "Quickly, Yusuf, hold it steady!" al-Biruni called, raising the astrolabe to his eye. He was measuring something so tiny that Yusuf could hardly believe it mattered: how far the horizon dipped below a perfectly level line. Yusuf's hands were shaking with excitement, but his teacher's were as steady as the rock beneath them.

On the way down, Yusuf finally plucked up the courage to ask what the tiny angle actually meant. "Think about it," al-Biruni said, drawing a circle in the dust with a stick. "If the Earth were flat, the horizon would be exactly level with my eye, but because the Earth is round, it curves away and the horizon drops slightly." He drew a line from the mountaintop to the edge of the circle, forming a long, thin triangle. "Once we know the height of the mountain and the size of that angle, the triangle will tell us everything else, including the distance to the centre of the Earth."

That night, by the light of a flickering oil lamp, they worked through page after page of calculations. Yusuf read out the numbers while his teacher checked them against his tables, muttering under his breath. Long after the fort had fallen silent, al-Biruni put down his pen and leaned back with a tired smile. According to his result, the radius of the Earth was about six thousand three hundred and forty kilometres in today's units. Almost a thousand years later, modern scientists using satellites would discover that he had been wrong by less than one percent.

Yusuf stepped outside into the cool night air, his head buzzing with numbers. A sleepy guard on the wall asked him what on earth the two of them had been doing all day. "We measured the world," Yusuf replied simply. The guard burst out laughing, clearly convinced that the apprentice had become as eccentric as his master. Yusuf did not mind in the least; he looked up at the stars, which no longer seemed quite so far away, and smiled to himself. For the first time, he understood that knowledge was not something you were given, but something you had to climb towards, one careful step at a time.

pages.text: For as long as Faisal could remember, the oud had been sitting on top of his grandmother's wardrobe, wrapped in a faded green cloth like a secret nobody wanted to tell. Nobody ever mentioned it, and somehow he had always known not to ask. It was the summer he turned fifteen, during a heatwave that kept everyone in Jeddah indoors, that his curiosity finally got the better of him. While his grandmother was taking her afternoon nap, he dragged a chair across the room and lifted the instrument down. When he pulled back the cloth, he saw a long crack running across its round wooden body, and a small leather notebook slipped out and landed at his feet.

The notebook was full of strange symbols: rows of numbers and Arabic letters that didn't look anything like the music Faisal had studied at school. He was still trying to make sense of them when he heard footsteps behind him. His grandmother, Noura, stood frozen in the doorway, her eyes fixed on the oud in his hands. "Your grandfather was writing something for me," she said quietly, after a long silence. "He worked on it for months, but he never got the chance to finish it." Faisal turned to the last page and saw that the lines of numbers simply stopped halfway down, followed by nothing but empty paper.

Faisal had never met his grandfather, Salem, who had been a fisherman with a famously loud laugh and, apparently, a secret talent for music. The next day, he took the notebook to Mr. Hamdan, his music teacher, hoping he could crack the code. Mr. Hamdan turned the pages slowly and gave a low whistle. "This is an old way of writing music for the oud," he explained. "Each number tells you which string to play and where to put your finger." Then he scribbled an address on a scrap of paper and said, "If anyone can help you, it's Abu Yousef, the instrument maker in Al-Balad."

The workshop was hidden down a narrow alley in the old city, between tall coral-stone houses with carved wooden balconies. Inside, the air smelled of sawdust and polish, and half-built instruments hung from the ceiling like sleeping bats. Abu Yousef, a small man with thick glasses, took one look at the oud and let out a delighted laugh. "I'd know this anywhere, because I made it myself, back in 1979!" he exclaimed. "Salem couldn't afford to pay me all at once, so he brought me fresh fish every Friday for six months."

Abu Yousef agreed to repair the oud on one condition: Faisal had to help with every step. For the next three weeks, Faisal spent his afternoons sanding thin strips of wood, mixing glue and learning that rushing a job only meant doing it twice. Meanwhile, the old man taught him to read the notebook, explaining that the melody was written in maqam Bayati, a scale that could sound both joyful and heartbreaking at the same time. Little by little, the strange numbers began to turn into music under Faisal's fingers. For the first time, he felt as if he were having a conversation with a man he had never met.

There was just one problem: the song still had no ending. Faisal tried dozens of possibilities, staying up late and recording himself on his phone, but every ending he invented sounded wrong, like wearing someone else's shoes. One evening, completely fed up, he pushed the notebook away and told Abu Yousef that he was ready to give up. The old man didn't argue; he simply polished his glasses and said, "Your grandfather didn't leave the ending in the notebook, my son. Perhaps he left it somewhere else." Faisal walked home that night turning those words over and over in his mind.

Instead of searching for notes, Faisal decided to search for memories, so he asked his grandmother to tell him about Salem. She talked for hours, about his terrible jokes, his patience with his nets and the way he always came home smelling of salt and sea. "Every evening, he would sit on our balcony facing the water and hum the same little tune," she said with a smile. "I teased him about it for forty years." Faisal asked her to hum it, and when she did, a little unsure at first, he suddenly realised that it fitted the last line of the notebook perfectly. The ending had been in her memory all along.

The repaired oud was ready just in time for Eid. That evening, the whole family gathered in his grandparents' living room, the smell of cardamom coffee and sweet maamoul filling the air. Faisal's hands were shaking as he tuned the strings, and for a terrible moment he thought he would forget everything. Then he began to play, and the melody rose and fell like waves, joyful and heartbreaking at the same time, exactly as Abu Yousef had promised. When he reached the final line, his grandmother's tune, she closed her eyes and the room went completely silent.

For a moment nobody moved, and then his grandmother reached over and squeezed his hand. "Now it's finished," she whispered, her eyes shining with tears. Later that night, Faisal opened the leather notebook to the first blank page and, after a moment's hesitation, began writing a melody of his own. At the top of the page, in careful letters, he wrote: For Salem, from the grandson you never met. The oud no longer sits on top of the wardrobe; instead, it hangs on the living room wall, where anyone can take it down and play.

pages.text: Every summer, fifteen-year-old Yousef worked in his grandfather's perfume shop in Al-Balad, the old heart of Jeddah, where coral-stone houses leaned over narrow lanes. The shop was tiny and dark, but it held the most precious thing his family owned: a square glass bottle of oud oil called Layali. It had been aged for forty years, and his grandfather refused to sell it, no matter how much he was offered. Yousef had smelled it only once, as a small boy, and the memory had never left him. It was deep and smoky, like a winter night in the desert.

One Thursday morning, a wealthy collector from Dubai arrived, hoping to persuade the old man to change his mind. Grandfather smiled politely, unlocked the glass cabinet and carefully removed the wax seal from Layali. The moment the bottle was opened, Yousef frowned. The scent was thin and sweet, with a cheap note of jasmine that had no business being there. "Grandfather," he whispered, "that isn't Layali." The old man raised the bottle to his nose, and his face turned as pale as paper.

After the embarrassed collector had left, Grandfather sank into his chair as if he had aged ten years in ten minutes. "Only two people have keys to that cabinet," he said quietly. "Me, and Saleem, who has kept my accounts for twenty years and is on holiday in Abha." That left Hamza, the shy assistant who had started working there a month earlier, as the obvious suspect. Grandfather wanted to avoid a scandal, so Yousef begged him to wait one day before calling the police. Reluctantly, the old man agreed.

Yousef soon noticed that Hamza seemed jumpy, avoiding his eyes whenever he spoke to him. Behind some boxes in the storeroom, Yousef discovered a folded blanket, a pillow and a phone charger. When he asked about them, Hamza's voice shook as he admitted he had lost his room and had been secretly sleeping in the shop. "On Tuesday night, I saw a light and heard someone at the cabinet," he confessed. "I assumed it was your grandfather, and I was too ashamed to come out."

That evening, Yousef smelled the fake oil again, and suddenly he remembered where he had come across that sugary jasmine before. It was a blend sold by Abu Nasser, who ran a cheerful little stall at the edge of the souq. Yousef went straight there and described the bottle. "Ah, yes," said Abu Nasser, stroking his beard. "On Tuesday morning, a man in sunglasses bought exactly that amount and asked me to make it as dark as possible."

The next morning, Saleem returned, looking relaxed and carrying a leather bag. He listened to the news with a shocked expression and shook his head sadly. "It must have been the new boy," he said gently. "You can never really know a stranger." While he was talking, Yousef glanced at the shop's ledger, and his heart skipped a beat: there was an entry dated Tuesday evening, written in Saleem's famous green ink.

Yousef took a deep breath and tried to keep his voice steady. "Uncle Saleem, you said you were in Abha all week, yet you wrote in the ledger on Tuesday," he began. "That same night, someone was seen at the cabinet, and that morning a man in sunglasses bought fake oil identical to what we found." Saleem laughed nervously and claimed he must have written the wrong date. Then Yousef leaned closer and said softly, "There's one more thing. Your bag smells of Layali."

For a long moment, nobody spoke, and then Saleem's shoulders dropped. With tears in his eyes, he explained that his own business had collapsed and he was drowning in debts he had been too proud to mention. He had planned to sell the oil abroad, but he had not yet found a buyer. Slowly, he opened his bag and placed the real Layali on the counter. "I have known you for twenty years," Grandfather said, his voice heavy with disappointment, "and you never once asked me for help."

Saleem left the shop that day for good, but Grandfather promised to help him find an honest way to repay his debts. Hamza was given a small room above the shop, and a proper salary to go with it. That night, Grandfather poured a single drop of Layali onto Yousef's wrist. "A good nose found the truth," he said, "but a good heart decided what to do with it." Yousef breathed in the deep, smoky scent and smiled, knowing he would never forget this summer.

pages.text: It started on a perfectly ordinary Tuesday, in the middle of a maths test that Faisal was quietly failing. At exactly 10:17, the school bell rang for one long minute, then fell silent. Thirty heads lifted at once, and Mr. Hamdan frowned at the clock as if it had personally insulted him. Break wasn't until 10:45, so nobody moved, but the whisper spread around the room like wildfire.

By the end of the week, the bell had rung at 10:17 every single day, and the rumours were getting wilder. Some boys claimed the school was haunted, while others insisted it was a secret fire drill. Faisal, who edited the school newsletter with his best friend Majed, saw an opportunity. "This is the story we've been waiting for," he said, tapping his notebook. "If we find out who's behind it, everyone will finally read what we write."

Faisal already had a suspect in mind: Tariq, a quiet boy from the year above who was famous for building robots and fixing anything with a screen. "He's been seen near the admin office twice this week," Faisal said. "It has to be him." Majed looked sceptical. "Seen by whom? You can't just jump to conclusions because someone is good with computers." But Faisal had already started scribbling a headline: Tech Genius Behind Bell Mystery?

To gather evidence, the boys stayed behind after school and went looking for Abu Nasser, the caretaker who had worked there for over thirty years. They found him in a dusty storeroom, sorting through boxes of old trophies and faded photographs. When Faisal asked about the bell, the old man's hands stopped moving. "So it's ringing again," he murmured, almost to himself. "I never thought I'd hear that sound one more time."

Abu Nasser pulled out a black-and-white photograph of a tall man standing proudly in front of the school gates. "This was Ustadh Ibrahim, our very first headmaster," he explained. "Every day at 10:17, he rang the bell for one minute so that students and teachers could stop, breathe, and think about something they were grateful for." The tradition had faded away after he retired, and eventually the old bell system had been switched off and forgotten. "Why 10:17?" Majed asked. "Because that was the exact minute the doors first opened," the caretaker replied with a smile.

The next morning, Faisal and Majed went straight to the IT department, where they were surprised to find Tariq helping the technician. Faisal felt his face turn hot as he remembered the headline in his notebook. Tariq explained that the school had recently installed a new digital system, and during the upgrade, an ancient backup file had been accidentally restored. "It's a glitch," he said, showing them the screen. "There's one line of programming from decades ago: ring at 10:17, sixty seconds, every school day."

Walking back to class, Faisal tore the page out of his notebook and crumpled it into a tight ball. "I nearly accused him in front of the whole school," he admitted, feeling thoroughly ashamed of himself. Majed shrugged kindly. "Nearly isn't the same as actually doing it. Real journalists check their facts, remember?" That afternoon, Faisal found Tariq in the corridor and apologised, and to his relief, Tariq simply laughed and asked if he could help with the article.

The three boys spent the weekend writing the true story of Ustadh Ibrahim and the forgotten minute of gratitude. Abu Nasser lent them the old photographs, and Tariq designed the layout so that it looked genuinely professional. When the newsletter came out, copies disappeared within an hour, and even the teachers were discussing it in the staffroom. By Thursday, the headmaster had called the boys into his office, and Faisal was sure they were in trouble.

Instead, the headmaster told them he had decided not to fix the glitch at all. From then on, the bell would ring at 10:17 on purpose, and the whole school would pause to remember what they were thankful for. On the first official day, Faisal watched Abu Nasser standing in the courtyard with his eyes closed and a peaceful smile on his face. Faisal had set out to catch a culprit, but he had found something far more valuable. When the minute ended, he quietly added one more thing to his list: friends who tell you the truth.

Personally, I'd go for the kitchen, because I learn faster when I'm doing something rather than just listening.

grammar.title: Linking contrasts: whereas, while, unlike
grammar.ar: نستخدم whereas و while لربط جملتين كاملتين متناقضتين، ويمكن وضعهما في بداية الجملة أو في وسطها. أما unlike فيأتي بعدها اسم أو ضمير وليس جملة كاملة. تجنّب استخدام but في كل مرة، فتنويع أدوات الربط يرفع درجتك في الامتحان.
examples: Whereas the first photo is taken indoors, the second one is outdoors.
The students in the library look focused, while the ones in the park seem more relaxed.
Unlike the girl in the first picture, the boy is working with a partner.

words.ar: يخمّن / يتوقّع بناءً على ما يراه
words.ex: In this part of the exam, you need to speculate about the people in the photos.
Judging by her smile, she's just received some good news.
He looks relieved that the exam is finally over.
She seems frustrated because the experiment didn't work.
They must be exhausted after climbing all morning.
His facial expression suggests he's quite nervous.

dialogue.t: Look at this photo. How do you think the people are feeling, and what has just happened?
Well, they're a team of students holding a trophy, so they must have just won some kind of competition, maybe a robotics contest.
What about the boy on the left?
I'd imagine he's feeling quite relieved, judging by the way he's leaning back and closing his eyes. He might have been worried that their robot would break down.
And the girl at the back?
It looks as though she's trying to call someone, perhaps her parents, to tell them the news. She can't have expected to win, because she looks genuinely shocked.
What do you think might happen next?
They'll probably go out to celebrate, and I suppose their teacher might take a photo for the school website.

grammar.title: Past modals of deduction
grammar.ar: نستخدم must have + التصريف الثالث للفعل عندما نكون شبه متأكدين أن شيئًا حدث في الماضي، و might/may/could have عندما نظن أنه ربما حدث، و can't have عندما نكون متأكدين أنه لم يحدث. انتبه: لا نقول mustn't have للاستنتاج، بل can't have. هذه الأفعال ضرورية لوصف ما حدث للتو في الصور.
examples: She must have just finished a race because she's out of breath.
They might have lost their way, judging by the map in their hands.
He can't have slept well; he looks completely exhausted.

words.ex: Schools should encourage students to read for pleasure.
Graphic novels might appeal to teenagers who don't like long books.
I'm not sure I'd go along with the idea of making reading compulsory.
Prizes can be a good incentive for younger students.
Peer pressure can actually be positive if your friends love reading.
Setting up a book club would definitely be worthwhile.

dialogue.t: So, here are some ways to encourage teenagers to read more. Shall we start with book clubs? How do you feel about that idea?
I think it's quite effective, actually. Talking about books with friends makes reading feel more social, and it might appeal to people who usually find it boring.
True. What about giving prizes to students who read the most books?
I'm not sure I'd go along with that, because students might just choose very short books to win. The incentive should be enjoying the story, not the prize.
That's a fair point. Shall we move on to inviting authors to schools?
Yes, I love that one. Meeting a real writer can be really inspiring. How do you feel about it?
I agree, although it might be expensive for some schools.
Maybe they could organise online talks instead. That would still be worthwhile and much cheaper.

grammar.title: Prepositions + -ing form
grammar.ar: بعد حروف الجر مثل about و of و on و in نستخدم الفعل بصيغة ing- وليس المصدر مع to. يخطئ كثير من المتحدثين بالعربية فيقولون: How do you feel about to give، والصحيح How do you feel about giving. تذكّر أن صيغة ing- هنا تعمل كاسم، تمامًا مثل المصدر في العربية.
examples: How do you feel about inviting authors to school?
I'm not convinced of the benefits of giving prizes.
Shall we move on to talking about reading apps?

words.ex: Let's narrow it down to two options first.
After a long discussion, we finally settled on the library idea.
Maybe we can reach a compromise and combine both ideas.
Reading apps might be more effective in the long run.
I think the benefits clearly outweigh the costs.
Online author talks are a cost-effective solution.

dialogue.t: Now you have a minute to decide which of these ideas would be the most effective.
OK, so, we seem to agree that prizes aren't really the answer. Shall we narrow it down to book clubs and author visits?
Good idea. Personally, I'd choose author visits, because they're so memorable.
I can see your point, but I still think book clubs would be more effective in the long run. A visit only happens once, whereas a club meets every week.
That's true. And book clubs are probably more cost-effective too.
Exactly. The benefits definitely outweigh the effort of organising it.
Right, so which one shall we settle on?
If we had to choose just one, it would have to be the book club. Maybe as a compromise, the club could invite an author once a year.

grammar.title: Second conditional for hypothetical choices
grammar.ar: نستخدم الشرط الثاني (If + الماضي البسيط، would + الفعل) للحديث عن مواقف افتراضية، مثل الاختيار النهائي في المهمة التعاونية. العبارة it would have to be تعني أن هذا هو الخيار الوحيد المنطقي في رأيك. لا تضع would في جملة if، فنقول If we had وليس If we would have.
examples: If we had to choose just one, it would have to be the book club.
If the school had more money, author visits would be the best option.
If I were the head teacher, I'd set up a reading corner in every classroom.

words.ex: I suppose it depends on the student's personality.
Generally speaking, teenagers spend too much time online.
Not every family has access to fast internet.
Online learning can increase inequality between rich and poor students.
On the other hand, technology makes learning more flexible.
Sport and art are essential for a well-rounded education.

dialogue.t: Do you think all students should learn online in the future?
That's an interesting question. I suppose it depends on the age of the students. Older students can manage their time, whereas younger children need a teacher in the room.
Some people say exams put too much pressure on young people. What's your opinion?
Generally speaking, I'd agree, although in some cases a bit of pressure can actually push you to work harder. The problem is when exams are the only thing that matters.
Should schools teach practical skills like managing money?
I've never really thought about it, but now that you mention it, yes. A well-rounded education should prepare you for real life, not just for tests.
And does technology make education fairer?
Well, on the one hand, it gives people access to free resources. On the other hand, not everyone has a laptop, so it could increase inequality.

grammar.title: Depend on + noun / wh-clause
grammar.ar: بعد depend نستخدم دائمًا on وليس of أو from، وهو خطأ شائع لدى المتحدثين بالعربية بسبب الترجمة الحرفية. يمكن أن يأتي بعد depends on اسم، أو جملة تبدأ بكلمة استفهام مثل how و whether و what. هذه البنية مفيدة جدًا لإعطاء رأي متوازن وكسب الوقت للتفكير.
examples: I suppose it depends on the type of school.
It really depends on how much support students get at home.
Whether online learning works depends on what subject you're studying.

words.ex: She took a firm stance against banning phones at school.
In my opinion, the benefits of a phone ban outweigh the drawbacks.
Constant notifications are a huge distraction during lessons.
We shouldn't overlook the fact that some students need phones for medical reasons.
He made a compelling argument for keeping phones in lockers.
It's difficult for teachers to enforce a rule that students keep breaking.

dialogue.t: So, should smartphones be banned during the school day? What's your position?
I'd argue that they should be banned, because they're a constant distraction in class.
But lots of students use their phones for research and for staying in touch with their parents.
While it's true that phones can be useful, we shouldn't overlook the fact that most students use them for social media during lessons.
Couldn't schools just set clear rules instead of imposing a total ban?
The way I see it, the benefits of a ban outweigh the inconvenience. Students would concentrate better and actually talk to each other at break.
That's a strong stance. But what about emergencies?
Schools have landlines, and phones could be kept in lockers so students can reach them if something serious happens.

grammar.title: Concessive clauses with 'While'
grammar.ar: نستخدم 'While' في بداية الجملة بمعنى 'مع أنّ' أو 'على الرغم من أنّ' لنعترف بفكرة الطرف الآخر قبل أن نقدّم رأينا الأقوى. يأتي بعد 'While' جملة كاملة (فاعل + فعل)، ثم فاصلة، ثم الجملة الرئيسية التي تحمل موقفنا. هذا الأسلوب يجعل حجتك تبدو متوازنة وأكثر إقناعاً. انتبه: لا نضيف 'but' بعد الفاصلة، فنقول: While it's true that..., we shouldn't... وليس While..., but we...
examples: While it's true that phones help with research, they also encourage cheating.
While some parents want constant contact, students need time to focus.
While I understand your concern, I still believe a ban is the best solution.

words.ex: I'll concede that online classes are more flexible.
Be ready to respond to your opponent's counterarguments.
That's a valid point, but it doesn't change my overall view.
Online learning offers flexibility for students who travel a lot.
Nothing can fully replace face-to-face interaction with a good teacher.
Studying from home requires a lot of self-discipline.

dialogue.t: I think online learning is the future. Students can study at their own pace.
Granted, online learning offers more flexibility, but most teenagers need a structured routine.
Online platforms can track your progress and give you instant feedback, though.
That's a fair point; however, feedback from a screen can't replace face-to-face interaction with a teacher.
Actually, many shy students feel more confident asking questions online.
Even if some students feel more comfortable online, it doesn't necessarily follow that they learn more effectively.
So you don't see any role for online learning at all?
I wouldn't go that far. It works well as a supplement, just not as a replacement for the classroom.

grammar.title: Conceding with 'Granted' and 'Even if'
grammar.ar: نستخدم 'Granted, ..., but ...' لنعترف بأن نقطة الطرف الآخر صحيحة، ثم نعارضها مباشرة بـ 'but'. أما 'Even if' فتعني 'حتى لو'، وتُستخدم لنقول إن النتيجة لا تتغير حتى لو كانت الفكرة صحيحة. لا تخلط بين 'Even if' (حتى لو - افتراض) و'Even though' (مع أنّ - حقيقة مؤكدة). العبارة 'it doesn't necessarily follow that' تعني 'هذا لا يعني بالضرورة أن...' وهي طريقة قوية لكشف ضعف المنطق.
examples: Granted, online courses are cheaper, but they can feel isolating.
Even if online exams are convenient, it doesn't necessarily follow that they're fair.
That's a fair point; however, not every family has a reliable internet connection.

words.ex: Some European city centres have become completely car-free.
Banning cars would inevitably change the way people shop.
The city would need better infrastructure, such as shaded walkways.

words.ar: شخص يتنقّل يومياً (إلى العمل أو الدراسة)
words.ex: Thousands of commuters use the metro every morning.
Traffic congestion wastes hours of people's time every week.
How would elderly people cope with walking long distances?

dialogue.t: Imagine Riyadh became completely car-free. If the city were to ban cars, it would inevitably cut air pollution.
Maybe, but supposing cars disappeared tomorrow, how would people cope with walking in the summer heat?
The metro would carry most commuters. Had the city not invested in the Riyadh Metro, we might never have considered this idea at all.
True, but it doesn't reach every neighbourhood. If families were to lose their cars, it would inevitably make school runs much harder.
Not if they expanded bus routes and built air-conditioned stops.
Supposing that happened, how would shops and restaurants cope with deliveries?
They could use small electric vans at night, like some European cities do.
I'm still not convinced, but I'll admit the congestion would disappear overnight.

grammar.title: Hypotheticals: 'were to' and inverted 'Had'
grammar.ar: نستخدم 'If + subject + were to + المصدر' للحديث عن موقف افتراضي في المستقبل يبدو بعيد الحدوث، وهي أكثر رسمية من 'If + الماضي البسيط'. أما 'Had + subject + past participle' فهي صيغة مقلوبة من الشرط الثالث تعني 'لو لم/لو أنّ ... في الماضي'، ونحذف فيها 'If'. مثلاً: Had they not built the metro = If they hadn't built the metro. هذه التراكيب تجعل أسلوبك في النقاش أكثر رقيّاً وإقناعاً.
examples: If the government were to ban cars, public transport would inevitably become overcrowded.
Had the city not built the metro, traffic would be even worse today.
Supposing petrol became very expensive, how would delivery companies cope?

words.ex: Regular exercise plays a big role in teenage wellbeing.
His claim is borne out by recent research.
A case in point is the school that added daily sport and saw grades improve.
Being part of a team can boost your self-esteem.
The findings suggest that active students sleep better.
Many teenagers say that running helps them manage anxiety before exams.

dialogue.t: Do you really think sport makes teenagers happier?
Definitely. According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression.
But that research might mainly be about adults.
Not really. This is borne out by studies of school students, which suggest that active teenagers tend to have higher self-esteem.
Statistics are one thing, but what about real life?
A case in point is my cousin. He joined a football team last year and he's far more confident now, which clearly shows that sport can change someone.
Couldn't that just be because he made new friends?
Partly, but that's exactly my point: team sport builds friendships, and friendships are a huge part of wellbeing.

grammar.title: Reporting evidence with passive structures
grammar.ar: في النقاش الجاد نستخدم المبني للمجهول لتقديم الأدلة بطريقة موضوعية، دون التركيز على الشخص. من التراكيب المفيدة: 'It has been shown that...' (ثبت أنّ...)، و'Studies are said to...'، و'This is borne out by...' (وهذا ما يؤكّده...). كما نستخدم 'According to + المصدر' لذكر مصدر المعلومة بوضوح. هذا يجعل ادعاءك يبدو مدعوماً بالحقائق لا مجرد رأي شخصي.
examples: It has been shown that teenagers who exercise regularly sleep better.
This is borne out by a survey of over a thousand students.
According to recent findings, team sports reduce feelings of loneliness.

words.ex: Sorry to cut in, but I think we're missing something important.
She held the floor until she had finished her argument.
A good moderator steers the conversation back to the main question.
We went off on a tangent and started talking about football.
Should volunteering be compulsory for secondary students?
You raised an interesting point about community service.

dialogue.t: I believe volunteering should be compulsory for all secondary students, because it teaches responsibility, and—
Sorry to cut in, but wouldn't forcing students defeat the whole purpose of volunteering?
If you'd just let me finish — even required volunteering exposes students to real problems in their community.
If I could just come back on what you said about responsibility, don't students learn that from part-time jobs too?
Possibly, but jobs are about money. Talking of money, some companies charge families a fortune for volunteering trips abroad...
Let's get back to the main issue, which is whether volunteering should be required at all.
Fair enough. My answer is yes, as long as students can choose the cause they support.
That's a compromise I could probably accept.

grammar.title: Softening interruptions with 'just' and 'could'
grammar.ar: عند مقاطعة شخص أو طلب الكلام في نقاش، نستخدم كلمات مخففة مثل 'just' و'could' و'if I may' حتى يبدو كلامنا مهذباً وليس عدوانياً. كلمة 'just' تقلل من حجم الطلب، و'If I could...' تجعله أشبه باستئذان. للاحتفاظ بالكلمة نقول مثلاً: 'If you'd just let me finish...' أو 'Let me just finish this point'. هذه العبارات مهمة جداً في المناقشات الجماعية واختبار المحادثة.
examples: If I could just add something here, volunteering also looks great on a CV.
Sorry to cut in, but could I just clarify what you mean by 'compulsory'?
Let me just finish this point, and then you can respond.

words.ex: On balance, I think homework does more good than harm.

words.ar: يتلخّص في / يرجع في جوهره إلى
words.ex: The whole debate boils down to how we use our time.

words.ar: بعد أخذ كل الأمور بعين الاعتبار
words.ex: All things considered, a shorter school day might be a good idea.
The main drawback of daily homework is the stress it causes.
Practice at home reinforces what students learn in class.
Too much homework can lead to burnout before exams.

dialogue.t: We've heard strong arguments on both sides. Would you like to give your closing statement?
Yes. Supporters of homework say it reinforces what we learn in class and builds discipline.
And what about the other side?
Opponents argue that too much homework leads to stress and burnout, and leaves no time for family or hobbies.
So where do you stand?
All things considered, homework does have value. On balance, I'm convinced that a small amount, focused on practice, is better than none at all.
Why not just get rid of it completely?
Because what it really boils down to is quality, not quantity. Twenty minutes of meaningful practice beats two hours of pointless busywork.

grammar.title: Emphasis with 'What' cleft sentences
grammar.ar: جملة 'What' المشطورة (cleft sentence) تُستخدم لإبراز الفكرة الأهم في نهاية الجملة، وهي مثالية للخاتمة الإقناعية. تركيبها: What + فاعل + فعل + is/was + الفكرة المهمة. مثلاً بدلاً من 'The debate boils down to quality' نقول: 'What it really boils down to is quality'. هذا الأسلوب يلفت انتباه المستمع ويجعل رسالتك الأخيرة قوية وواضحة.
examples: What really matters is how useful the homework is.
What I find most convincing is the evidence about stress levels.
What students need is time to rest as well as time to practise.

words.ex: Hegra was the first heritage site in Saudi Arabia to be added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
More than a hundred tombs were carved into the sandstone cliffs by the Nabataeans.
The view of the rock formations at sunset is absolutely breathtaking.
A surprising fact at the start can captivate your audience within seconds.
The Nabataeans were an ancient civilisation that controlled important trade routes.
How the tombs were built without modern tools still intrigues historians today.

dialogue.t: Can I try my opening on you? I want it to sound less like a textbook.
Sure, go ahead. I'll pretend I've never heard of AlUla.
Okay. Have you ever wondered why a desert valley in north-west Saudi Arabia attracts visitors from all over the world?
Nice, that question definitely makes me want to know the answer. What comes next?
Picture this: you're standing in front of a huge tomb carved into a golden cliff, and it's over two thousand years old.
That's really vivid. Maybe pause after 'picture this' so people have time to imagine it.
Good idea. Then I'll say: Today, I'd like to walk you through the history of Hegra, its Nabataean tombs and why it still matters to us.
Perfect. You've hooked me, and I know exactly what the talk will cover.

grammar.title: Rhetorical questions and imperatives for openings
grammar.ar: نستخدم السؤال البلاغي مثل Have you ever wondered why...? لإثارة فضول الجمهور دون انتظار إجابة حقيقية. لاحظ أن ترتيب الكلمات بعد why يكون ترتيب جملة خبرية وليس سؤالاً، فنقول why it attracts وليس why does it attract. ويُستخدم فعل الأمر مثل Picture this أو Imagine لدعوة المستمع إلى تخيّل مشهد ما. ثم نختم المقدمة بعبارة تحدد محتوى العرض مثل Today, I'd like to walk you through...
examples: Have you ever wondered why the Nabataeans chose such a remote place to build their tombs?
Picture this: the sun is rising over the sandstone cliffs and the whole valley is glowing orange.
Today, I'd like to walk you through three reasons why AlUla deserves its global reputation.

words.ex: Our school launched an initiative to clean up the local beach every month.
First, I'll briefly outline how the project started.
Could you elaborate on how you persuaded people to volunteer?
The tree-planting project is ongoing, and we hope to plant five hundred more trees.
One positive outcome was that neighbours started talking to each other more.
In terms of funding, the project relied entirely on local businesses.

dialogue.t: So far I've explained how our neighbourhood garden project started. Turning now to the challenges we faced, the biggest one was water.
That makes sense in our climate. How did you deal with it?
We installed a drip irrigation system, which cut our water use by almost half.
Impressive. Will you say more about that in the talk?
Yes. Let me elaborate on the irrigation system for a moment, because people always ask about it.
Good. And after the challenges, what's the final section?
This brings me to my next point, which is the impact on the community, especially on elderly residents who now meet there every evening.
Your transitions are really clear. I never felt lost between sections.

grammar.title: Signposting and non-defining relative clauses
grammar.ar: عبارات الربط مثل Turning now to... وThis brings me to my next point تساعد المستمع على معرفة الانتقال من قسم إلى آخر في العرض. بعد Turning now to نستخدم اسماً أو صيغة الفعل مع ing. وفي عبارة This brings me to my next point, which is... نستخدم جملة وصفية غير محددة تبدأ بـ which وتُفصل بفاصلة لإضافة معلومة توضيحية عن النقطة.
examples: Turning now to the results, we collected over two tonnes of rubbish in six months.
This brings me to my next point, which is how we kept volunteers motivated.
Let me elaborate on the role of local businesses for a moment.

words.ex: Saudi hospitality is famous among visitors from all over the world.
It's customary to stand up when an older person enters the room.
Serving the eldest guest first is a sign of respect.
Shaking the cup is a small gesture with a clear meaning.
Families usually break the fast with dates and water at sunset.
Eid is a time for large family gatherings and visits to relatives.

dialogue.t: In your last message you mentioned Arabic coffee. Is it just a drink, or is there more to it?
There's a lot more to it. It's customary to serve coffee with dates as soon as guests arrive.
Interesting. Does it matter who gets served first?
Yes, the host usually starts with the oldest or most important guest. Offering coffee is traditionally seen as a sign of generosity and respect.
And how do you say you don't want any more? In the UK we'd just say 'no thanks'.
Unlike in the UK, people here tend to gently shake the small cup from side to side. That tells the host you've had enough.
What a neat gesture! I'd never have guessed that.
And during Ramadan, it's customary to break the fast with dates and water before the main meal.

grammar.title: Describing customs: impersonal it and passive reporting
grammar.ar: نستخدم It's customary to + الفعل المجرد لوصف عادة اجتماعية بشكل عام دون تحديد فاعل. ونستخدم صيغة المبني للمجهول is seen as + اسم لنقل نظرة المجتمع إلى شيء ما، مثل is traditionally seen as a sign of. وللمقارنة بين ثقافتين نستخدم Unlike in + اسم البلد، ثم tend to + الفعل للتعبير عن سلوك شائع غالباً وليس دائماً.
examples: It's customary to remove your shoes when you enter someone's home.
Refusing food at a gathering is often seen as slightly impolite.
Unlike in many Western countries, people here tend to eat dinner quite late.

words.ex: She paused to build suspense before revealing what happened.
Once the sun set, the desert was pitch-black.
We were stranded for hours after our car got stuck in the sand.
To my relief, my phone still had a little battery left.
A truck appeared out of nowhere and stopped beside us.
Volunteering at the food bank was an unforgettable experience.

dialogue.t: You said your family camping trip didn't go to plan. What happened?
We'd been driving through the desert for about three hours when suddenly the car sank into soft sand.
Oh no! Were you completely stranded?
Pretty much. No sooner had my dad started digging than the sun went down and everything turned pitch-black.
That sounds terrifying. How did you get out?
A truck appeared out of nowhere. To our relief, the driver was a local guide and he pulled us out in minutes.
What a story! Did it put you off camping?
Not at all. Looking back, I realise that it was the most unforgettable trip we've ever had.

grammar.title: Past perfect continuous and inversion with No sooner
grammar.ar: نستخدم الماضي التام المستمر had been + فعل ing لوصف حدث استمر فترة في الماضي قبل أن يقاطعه حدث مفاجئ بالماضي البسيط. أما No sooner had + فاعل + التصريف الثالث + than فتعني ما إن حدث كذا حتى حدث كذا، وتُستخدم لإضافة التشويق. لاحظ أن الفعل المساعد had يأتي قبل الفاعل بعد No sooner وهذا يسمى القلب.
examples: I'd been waiting at the airport for two hours when suddenly my name was announced.
No sooner had we arrived at the farm than it started pouring with rain.
Looking back, I realise that helping others taught me more than any lesson at school.

words.ex: My grandfather loves to reminisce about his childhood in old Jeddah.
Neighbourhoods used to be very close-knit, and everyone knew each other.
Back in the day, there were no shopping malls in our city.
New roads and buildings have completely transformed Riyadh.
She pointed out that families used to share meals with their neighbours.

words.ar: على ما يبدو / حسب ما يُقال
words.ex: Apparently, my grandmother walked to school every day.

dialogue.t: Did you manage to interview your grandmother for the project?
Yes, and she had so much to say. She told me that our street had been just sand when she first moved there.
Really? It's full of shops and traffic now.
I know. She pointed out that families used to leave their doors open all day because everyone trusted each other.
That sounds like a very close-knit community. What about entertainment?
Apparently, back then, people would gather on rooftops in the evening to escape the heat and chat.
Did she say whether she prefers life now or then?
She said she missed the old closeness, but she admitted that life was much easier today.

grammar.title: Reported speech: backshifting, used to and would
